# Head to Head — Preference by Comparison

> ⚠️ **Not scheduled.** For after the metadata campaign, when the downloaded images are complete. Recorded 2026-08-08.
> 
> 🔴 **Opinions are marked.** The operator asked for strong recommendations rather than a menu, so where I think there is a right answer I have said so and given the reasoning. Disagree with any of them and the design still stands.
## The evidence this is worth building
|  | Total | Rated by hand |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Actors | 1,100 | **2** (0%) |
| Videos | 2,104 | **8** (0%) |
| Videos *reviewed* | 2,104 | 791 (37%) |
⭐ **The rating field is dead on both, while the binary review flag is used on 37% of videos.** That is not indifference to quality — it is the cost of the question. "Reviewed or not" is one bit. "How many stars out of five" demands an absolute judgement against an imagined scale, and people are famously bad at it and slow to do it.
**"Which of these two?" is a question anyone answers instantly.** The feature is not a game bolted onto the data; it is a better elicitation method that happens to be fun.
Material is ready: **98% of actors have a primary photo, 85% a gallery.**
## D1 — One mechanic, two subjects
At the operator's direction the same game runs over **actors or videos**. The design is therefore about *comparable things*, not about actors.
What differs per subject is only **how a contender is presented**:
| Subject | Shows | Tap advances through |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Actor | Primary photo | Their gallery |
| Video | Contact-sheet frame | The other frames |
⚠️ **A video never autoplays here.** The game is a rapid visual judgement; audio and playback belong to the player, and a video that starts talking mid-session ends the session.
## D1b — The game starts by choosing WHO is in it
Added at the operator's direction. Before playing, pick the pool: gender, country, hair colour and traits for actors; studio, series, tags and cast for videos — whatever is relevant to the medium.
⭐ **This needs almost no new work.** `ActorFilterCriteria` and `AssetFilterCriteria` already exist, are already shared across screens, and already carry exactly these dimensions. The game gets a filter step by reusing the builder, not by inventing one.
⭐ And it makes the ranking **tractable**. A pool of sixty is rankable in a handful of sessions; 1,100 is not. Filtering is what turns "rank everything" into something that finishes.
### 🔴 One score, always. Filters choose who you SEE, not which ladder they are on.
⚠️ This is the decision the feature turns on, and the tempting answer is wrong.
It is tempting to keep a separate score per filter — "my ranking of this studio's videos". **Do not.** Two ladders cannot be compared afterwards, a contender's score would depend on which session they happened to appear in, and the operator would end up with a dozen incomparable rankings and no answer to "who do I actually like".
A filter says *what I feel like ranking today*. It is not a separate universe.
### ⚠️ The honest limitation this creates
If a pool is only ever played against itself, its contenders never meet anyone outside it — and scores between two pools that have never met are **not really comparable**, however much they share a scale. This is a genuine property of comparison-based ranking, not an implementation shortcut.
Mitigations, in order of honesty:
1. **Say so.** A leaderboard drawn from a pool that has barely met the rest should show its comparison counts rather than implying a settled global order.
2. D4's occasional distant pairing already helps — within a filter.
3. 🔴 **Offer an unfiltered mode and make it the default.** Filters are for when the operator wants them; a default that quietly fragments the ladder would produce exactly the incomparable mess this decision exists to avoid.
⚠️ **Do not attempt to "normalise" across disconnected pools.** It is a real statistical problem, the corrections are unintuitive, and a wrong correction is worse than an honest caveat.
## 🔴 D2 — Accumulate a score. Do NOT award a rating per run.
**This is the one part of the original sketch I would change.**
The sketch was: a run of ten, and the winner gets a star rating. ⚠️ That throws away almost everything the run learned and produces an unstable number — **the winner of a weak pool is not equivalent to the winner of a strong one**, so two runs produce inconsistent ratings for comparable contenders.
⭐ Instead: **every comparison nudges BOTH contenders**, by an amount that depends on how surprising the result was. Beating a high scorer moves you a lot; beating a low one barely moves you at all. An Elo-style update, which is a dozen lines.
What this buys:
- **No run boundary is needed** for a score to mean something
- Losers keep their information instead of being discarded
- The ranking **improves with every tap**, forever, rather than resetting
- Two sessions weeks apart compose correctly
🔴 **Star ratings are DERIVED from the distribution, never awarded.** Top decile is five stars, and so on — recomputed as the picture changes rather than frozen at the moment a run happened to end.
## 🔴 D3 — The game gets its own field. It never writes `rating`.
⚠️ `rating` is where the operator states an opinion. A score inferred from a game is **evidence**, not a statement, and the two must not compete — the same rule that keeps a source's description out of `Asset.notes`.
So: a separate `preferenceScore` (plus a comparison count), and `rating` stays exactly as hand-set as it is today.
🔴 **Deriving stars into ****`rating`**** is an explicit, reviewable action** — never a side effect of playing. "Apply these as ratings" should show what would change and be refusable.
⚠️ The conflict is theoretical today at 2 and 8 hand ratings. It costs nothing to get right now and cannot be retrofitted after the field is polluted.
## 🔴 D4 — Pair by similar score, not at random
⭐ **This decides whether the feature works.** Random pairs waste taps on obvious mismatches — comparing a clear favourite against a clear also-ran teaches almost nothing, because the answer was already known.
Pairing contenders with **close current scores** extracts the most information per tap. It is the difference between ranking 1,100 actors in fifty sessions and in five hundred.
⚠️ With a caveat: **pure score-matching never re-tests across tiers**, so an early mistake can strand someone. Mix in an occasional distant pairing — roughly one in five — to keep the ladder connected.
## 🔴 D5 — Endless and stoppable, not a fixed run of ten
The sketch proposed runs of ten. ⭐ With D2 there is **no reason for a run to end** — the score is always current, so any tap is a complete unit of work.
So: play as long as you like, stop whenever, nothing is lost or pending. ⚠️ A forced run of ten makes stopping at seven feel like waste, which is the opposite of what a low-friction elicitation tool wants.
🔴 If a sense of progress is wanted, give it a **session tally** ("14 compared") rather than a required length.
## 🔴 D6 — "Too close to call" is an ANSWER, and it is recorded
⚠️ Forcing a choice between two contenders someone genuinely rates equally injects noise into every score they touch. A draw is real information: it says these two belong at the same level.
Record it as a draw — both scores converge slightly — rather than discarding the comparison.
🔴 **"Neither" needs to exist too**, and means something different: neither belongs in this ranking at all. It should be possible to retire a contender from the game without rating them.
## D7 — Undo, because a mis-tap is inevitable
A fast tapping game on a phone produces mis-taps. ⚠️ Without undo, a mis-tap silently corrupts two scores and the operator learns not to trust the result.
One step back is enough, and it must reverse the score change, not merely re-show the pair.
## 🔴 D8 — Show confidence, and do not derive stars too early
⚠️ A score from three comparisons is not a score from thirty, and presenting them identically is the fastest way to make the whole ranking untrustworthy.
Each contender carries its **comparison count**. 🔴 Below a threshold — ten is a reasonable start — the score is shown as provisional and **contributes no derived star rating at all**.
⭐ This also gives the pairing rule something useful to do: prefer contenders with **few comparisons**, so coverage grows rather than the same familiar faces recurring.
## D9 — Cold start
- A contender with no score starts at the middle of the range.
- ⚠️ **A hand-set ****`rating`****, where one exists, seeds the starting score.** Ignoring an explicit statement in favour of a default would be perverse — and there are 10 of them across both subjects, so it costs nothing to honour.
- A contender with **no image cannot play**, and is excluded rather than shown blank. 98% of actors qualify today.
## What makes it fun rather than a chore
Stated because it is a design constraint, not decoration:
- **The next pair is prefetched.** A wait between taps ends the session faster than anything else.
- **No wrong answers, no score shown mid-game.** The moment it feels like a test it stops being a game.
- **A visible payoff.** A leaderboard worth reaching — "your top 20" — is the reason to keep playing, and it is also the feature's actual output.
## Test strategy (Constitution Art. III)
- **T1** — A win moves both contenders: winner up, loser down.
- **T2** — Beating a much higher scorer moves the winner MORE than beating a lower one.
- **T3** — A draw converges two scores and never diverges them.
- **T4** — Undo restores both scores exactly, including the comparison counts.
- **T5** — 🚨 The game NEVER writes `rating`. Asserted directly, because it is the one irreversible interaction with operator-authored data.
- **T6** — A contender below the confidence threshold yields no derived star.
- **T7** — Pairing prefers close scores, and still produces occasional distant pairs.
- **T8** — A contender with no image is never offered.
- **T9** — A hand-set rating seeds the initial score.
- **T10** — Scores are stable across sessions: the same comparisons in a different order reach the same ordering.
- **T11** — A filtered session updates the SAME scores an unfiltered one does; there is no per-filter ladder.
- **T12** — A filter yielding fewer than two eligible contenders is refused with a reason, not entered and then stuck.
## ❓ Open question — and it shapes the rest
**What is the ranking FOR?**
| Purpose | What it needs |
| --- | --- |
| Dashboard shelves, smart collections | Only a reliable TOP TIER — fifty contenders, quickly reached |
| "Who do I actually like", browsable | Broad coverage — many more sessions |
| Prioritising enrichment or photo work | The opposite end: which contenders you care LEAST about |
🔴 **My recommendation: build for the top tier first.** It is reachable in a handful of sessions, it is immediately useful on the Dashboard, and it is the version most likely to actually get played — which is the only way any of the others ever happen.
✅ decision - I agree. Top tier first but who I like and what I can discover about them is interesting.

# 🕸️ WHAT THIS UNLOCKS — preference across the graph
Raised by the operator: *"you like these videos and they're all from this studio, maybe you'd like these other videos from the same studio… or the same actor."*
⭐ **This is the payoff, and it is why the score belongs on the node rather than in a session log.** *What the Graph Could Answer* already proposed *"more like this by path, not by string"* — distance over shared performers, studio, family and tags. What it lacked was a **direction**: similar to *what*? A preference score supplies it, turning an undirected similarity measure into a recommendation.
⚠️ **It should become its own spec.** This game PRODUCES a signal; recommendation CONSUMES it. Different feature, different design questions, and folding them together would mean neither ships. Noted here because it justifies decisions above — particularly the single global score.
## 🔴 The opinions I already hold about it
### Preference propagates; it does not merely aggregate
Rating five of a studio's videos highly says something about **the studio**, which in turn says something about its other videos — including ones never compared. That is a graph traversal, not a filter.
🚨 **But an inferred score must never be confused with an elicited one.** `preferenceScore` comes from comparisons the operator actually made. A predicted score is a *guess about* them. Same rule as everywhere in this project: evidence and statement stay in separate fields, and the derived one is never written back over the real one.
### ⚠️ Confounding is the hard part, and the naive version gets it wrong
If five favourites share a studio, they very likely also share an actor, a tag and an era. **"Same studio" is only the explanation you happened to look at first.**
⭐ The honest version asks which dimension **best explains** the ratings — comparing how much each shared attribute accounts for, rather than reporting the first one found. That is the difference between a recommendation and a horoscope, and it is most of the work.
### The graph can say WHY, and should
⭐ *"Because you rated four videos with this performer highly"* is a defensible recommendation. One that cannot explain itself cannot be corrected — and a wrong recommendation the operator cannot argue with is one they stop trusting entirely.
⚠️ This is also the strongest argument for doing it on the graph rather than by any opaque method: the edges ARE the explanation.
### Losers are signal too
Head-to-head produces a ranking, not a list of favourites. **Consistently low-ranked contenders are as informative as high ones** — and a recommender that ignores them will keep proposing things already rejected, which is the fastest way to make it feel broken.
### Cold start applies again
⚠️ Predictions need the same confidence threshold as derived stars. A recommendation drawn from three comparisons is noise wearing a graph's clothing, and shipping that would discredit the feature before it had a chance.
## ⭐⭐ And beyond the library — "what else are they in that I do not have?"
Raised by the operator: *"you really liked this actor — let's query the source and see what else they're in that you don't have."*
🚨 **This is a different KIND of feature from everything else in this project.** Every tool so far describes, corrects or connects what the library already contains. This one tells the operator about things that are **not there** — the first time the app looks outward.
### ⭐ Why it is possible now and was not last week
The hard part is not asking the source what a performer appears in. It is answering **"do I already have this?"**
| Before match edges | Now |
| --- | --- |
| Fuzzy title comparison — a guess, wrong often enough to be useless | ⭐ An **exact lookup**: does any `video_match` row carry this scene's id? |
⭐ `knownWorks(actorId:limit:)` — built for the disambiguation picker — already fetches a performer's scenes. The diff against `video_match` is the only new logic.
### 🚨 The accuracy is bounded by how much of the library is identified
A video with no identity edge is **invisible to this check** and will be reported as missing even when it is sitting on disk.
On the drive library today: **1,074 of 2,104 videos carry an identity.** So roughly half the library cannot answer "I already have this", and a gap list built now would over-report badly.
⚠️ **This feature's usefulness is a direct function of the matching campaign finishing.** It should not be built — and certainly not judged — before then, or it will be dismissed as inaccurate when it is merely early.
### 🔴 It produces a list, and nothing more
The app should say *"these exist and you do not have them"* and stop there. No fetching, no acquiring, no links followed automatically — consistent with the no-background-network posture and with the write path being out of scope.  ✅ I agree
⚠️ **Ask only about contenders the operator actually ranked highly.** A sweep across 1,100 performers is a rate-limit problem and answers a question nobody asked; the top tier is a few dozen requests and answers the question they did.
⭐ That is a second, independent argument for D-open's recommendation to **build for the top tier first** — it is the only part of the ranking this feature needs.
⚠️ Also its own spec. Three features are now stacked on this signal — the game, graph recommendation, and this — and each has its own decisions.
## What the existing graph already supports
No new edges are needed. `video_performer`, `video_studio`, `video_tag`, `studio_parent` and `performer_tag` are already populated — 2,367 / 1,816 / 2,556 / 115 / 368 rows on the drive library — and the studio hierarchy means a preference for a network can reach the videos of its imprints.
⭐ **The graph work of the past two days is the prerequisite, and it is already done.** What is missing is only the preference signal, which is what this spec produces.
